analysis.one_liner: Exempts small-business ticket agents from rules requiring refunds for cancelled or badly delayed flights.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law requires airlines and ticket agents to refund passengers when a flight is cancelled or significantly delayed or changed. This bill would carve out an exemption: a ticket agent that qualifies as a small business under Small Business Administration rules would no longer have to give those automatic refunds. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Small ticket agents — travel agencies and similar sellers of airline tickets that qualify as small businesses — gain because they would no longer be required to hand back passengers' money when flights are cancelled, severely delayed, or significantly changed. Refunds can be a large cash-flow cost for a small business that fronts tickets on behalf of airlines.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a 'special rule for small businesses' to 49 U.S.C. § 42305(e) so the refund requirement 'shall not apply to a ticket agent that is a small business (as determined by the Administrator of the Small Business Administration).'

This would relieve small ticket agents of the obligation to refund passengers for cancelled or significantly delayed or changed flights, a cost that arises when the airline — not the agent — cancels or disrupts the flight.

analysis.who_pays: Passengers who buy tickets through a small ticket agent would lose their automatic right to a cash refund when a flight is cancelled, significantly delayed, or significantly changed; they would have to negotiate with the agent or the airline instead. They might not know their seller is a small business exempt from the rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Travelers who buy through small ticket agents

drawbacks.text: Travelers buying through a small ticket agent would lose the statutory refund guarantee that applies to everyone else, and there is no requirement that agents tell customers they are exempt — so a passenger may not discover this until a flight is cancelled.

The good-faith case for the bill is fairness to small firms: the agent often has no control over the airline's cancellation and has already passed the fare to the carrier, so requiring the agent to front refunds can strain a small business's cash flow while large online agencies absorb it easily.
The exemption creates uneven rules in the marketplace: identical tickets bought from a large seller versus a small seller would carry different refund rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to small ticket agents is real but narrow — relief from fronting refunds for disruptions they don't cause. The cost falls on the least-protected travelers, who would lose an automatic refund right with no clear notice of the exemption. On balance, the bill shifts risk from small businesses onto individual passengers buying the same flights.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Aviation Subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar introduced the Flight Refund Fairness Act on September 12, 2024, joined by Reps. Dina Titus and Mark Alford.
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day, and the next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.
No further action — no subcommittee vote, full committee markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Eight members cosponsored the bill: 3 House Democrats and 5 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no exemption was ever created. Travelers kept the existing guarantee that ticket agents must refund cancelled or significantly delayed or changed flights. Small ticket agents remain subject to the refund rule they sought relief from.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Travelers, who keep automatic refund rights

for.name: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt small-business ticket agents from the flight refund requirement.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Aviation Subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican with original support from a Democrat, and the eight cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 5 Republicans; no votes were ever taken, so no opposition record exists.

industries.note: The bill would exempt them from the statutory duty to refund passengers for cancelled or significantly delayed or changed flights, relieving their cash flow. That gain comes directly out of travelers' refund rights, since passengers would have no automatic recourse through the agent.

industries.industry: Large ticket sellers and online travel agencies
industries.note: They would remain subject to the refund requirement, keeping a compliance cost their smaller competitors would shed — and the same refund duty is also a consumer protection that applies to their customers. The bill does not change their obligations.
